24. In the case of Sultana Nahar vs Bangladesh and others reported in 1998 BLD 363 = 2 BLC 430 hundreds of sex workers were evicted unlawfully. Writ was filed against the Government of Bangladesh and Others for same reliefs including direction to rehabilitate them. One of the learned Judges of the Division Bench discharged the Rule as not maintainable while the Rule was made absolute by the other Judge. The learned Judge while giving dissenting judgment stated that since the action done was not in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a legal authority it does not come under the mischief of Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. On a reference to the third Judge, the dissenting decision was upheld. 

 41. In the case of M Saleem Ullah vs MdAbdur Rouf, Chief Election Commissioner and others reported in 1 BLC 229, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause under what authority respondent No.1, Mr Justice Md Abdur Rouf, had been holding the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh under Article 94 of the Constitution and also to show cause under what authority he was holding the office of the Chief Election Commissioner of Bangladesh under Artiele 118 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. It was held that since Mr Justice Md. Abdur Rouf returned to his earlier office as a Judge of the High Court Division and he was thereafter elevated to the Appellate Division as a Judge Rule did not subsist as it became infructuous.

 53. It is well known that there are certain important differences in the theory of interpretation of a Constitution contrasted with the theory of interpretation of statutes. The interpretation of a Constitution involves more than a passing interest concerning the actual litigants and being a pronouncement of the Court on the government and administration, has a more general and far reaching consequence. I feel tempted to quote the Chief Justice Marshal of the American Supreme Court warning in McCulloch vs Maryland. 4 Wheaton 316 which runs as under: 

 58. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq however, dismisses such argument as misplaced and irrelevant and submits that since the proviso to clause (3) of Article 147 permits such office, post or position to be retained by the President, Prime Minister, Minister, etc to hold otherwise would be an infraction of constitutional provision. I find good deal of force in the submission of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. In the language of the Chief Justice Marshall, the Court is not free to stretch or pervert the language of the Constitution in the interest of any legal or constitutional theory, or even for the purpose of supplying omissions or for the purpose of correcting supposed errors in the Constitution. Ours is by far a democratic' Constitution. Bangladesh Constitution by inserting a proviso to clause (2) of Article 56 has allowed technocrats to be appointed Ministers even though they .are not Members of Parliament. This may appear to be undemocratic but not unconstitutional. Similarly, the provision of Non party Caretaker Government in Chapter IIA (Article 58B-58E) of the Constitution may also appear to be undemocratic. But these provisions have been incorporated in our Constitution in the recent past as a painful necessity. 

 70. Relying upon Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Mr Akhtar Imam, Learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain as soon as he entered upon the office of a Minister on 23rd June, 1996 the said Article Came into play on him and by operation of this Article he lost all offices of profit disqualifying himself further to take any part in the management and conduct of those offices. According to him, the posts of Editor, Printer and Publisher in the Daily Ittefaq and the post of Executive Director-II in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd are all posts of profit. Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited provide that the object of the Company amongst others, was to make profit by running the going concerns namely, the New Nation Printing Press, the Daily Ittefaq, the weekly Purbani and the weekly Dhaka Times and, as such, these posts carrying emoluments are posts of profit. Mr Anwar Hossain therefore, lost these posts ipso facto on 23rd June, 1996 by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution. Since clause (3) of Article 147 provides that the persons to whom this Article applies shall not hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object, and clause (4) of the said Article provides that the Article applies to the offices of (a) President; (b) Prime Minister or the Chief Adviser: (c) Speaker or Deputy Speaker: (d) Minister or Adviser, Minister of State or Deputy Minister; (e) Judge of the Supreme Court; (i) Comptroller and Auditor General; (g) Election Commissioner: (h) Member of the Public Service Commission: the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain being a Minister was incapable of taking any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of the company named the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited and thus his actions appointing Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in- charge of the Daily Ittefaq, which is one of the subject matters of Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996, and order of re-instatement of Mr Monowarul Islam, Chief Accountant on 25-9-1999, suspension order of Md Habibullah, the Senior Security Officer of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd dated 23-1-1999 and order of appointment of Mr Shawkat Hossain Masum as in-charge of Finance Page of the Daily Ittefaq dated 17-8-1999 and subsequent cancellations of those orders by this respondent on 19-2-2000 which are subject matters of Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999, are all ilIegal, void, without jurisdiction and malafide, for at the time of issuing those orders and cancellations thereof the respondent was holding the office of a Minister and has illegally and in violation of Constitutional provisions taken part in the management and conduct of the Company. 

 76. In support of his contentions, Mr Akhtar Imam had relied upon the cases of Motahar Hossain Siddiqui vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR 238, Shahid Nabi Malik vs Chief Election Commissioner and others PLD 1997 (SC) 32. Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir and others vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 319, M Saleem Ullah, Advocate vs Justice Mohammad Abdul Quddus Chowdhury and another, reported in 46 DLR 691, an unreported Judgment in the case of Mainul Hosein vs Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others in Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994. 

 78. Mr Mahmudul Islam has commented that "The holders of offices of the President, Prime Minister, Speaker, Minister, Minister of State, Deputy Minister, Judge of the Supreme Court. Comptroller and Auditor-General. Election Commissioner and Members of the Public Service Commission (Mr Islam has inadvertently omitted the offices of Chief Adviser and Adviser which have been added in this list by amendment) may perform their duties free of any consideration except that of the public interest. Article 147(3) provides that no person appointed to or acting in any such office shall hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take part in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its objects. These may prevent the holder of any such office from receiving the salary or remuneration of the office as payment of salary or remuneration of the office renders such an office an office of profit, To remove any such contention a proviso has been included which states that for the purpose of clause (3), holders of these offices shall not be deemed to hold any office of profit even though they will receive the salary and other benefits of the office prescribed by Acts of Parliament in terms of Article 147(1). 

 92. His Lordship Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, (the former Chief Justice of Bangladesh) has precisely dealt with these types of questions in his book. "Bangladesh Constitution; Trends and Issues." In Chapter IX. page 159 the author wrote. "Each generation of lawyers and Judges grapple with specific issues confronting them. The entire Constitution is not thrown up for legal dissection all at a time. A Constitution unfolds itself in its beauties and deficiencies as time unfolds." In discussing the "Presumption and validity of statutes," the author has quoted the relevant portion of the judgment delivered by His Lordship Mr Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed (the former Chief Justice of Bangladesh) which says," A Constitution of Government is a living and organic thing which all instruments have the greatest claim to be construed" (reference is to Gwyer,CJ, AIR 1939 FC I in the case of Dr Nurul 1slam vs Bangladesh, 1981 BLD (AD) 140 (para 129). In Chapter- V page 85 the author wrote that "It will be important to remember that the Supreme Court of Bangladesh had very little occasion and opportunity to interpret the Constitution in its various facets and phases owing to frequent eclipse of the Constitution itself and owing to frequent interruptions with its Constitutional Jurisdiction. The Supreme Court interpreted the Constitution in fits and starts, as and when occasion permitted. The development of Constitutional law in Bangladesh was thwarted in its infancy. But looking at the crop of Constitutional cases which sprang up during the interlude (1979-82) one can safely conclude that had the Supreme Court been left free to do its work uninterruptedly the Constitution would have received a much more comprehensive and intensive interpretation in its hands." To trace the historical background as to how the development of Constitutional law in Bangladesh was thwarted in its infancy the author wrote, "The Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 made the first surgery on the powers of the High Court Division. Its power under Article 102(1) to issue directions. Orders, etc. for enforcement of fundamental rights was taken away, gone was the fundamental right to move the High Court Division for enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 44. Fundamental rights were to be enforced (in future) by a Constitutional Court. Tribunal or Commission which may be established by parliament by law (page 34). The Fourth Amendment came into force on the 25th January 1975. A new Part VIA was inserted in the Constitution, providing for the formation of a National Party to the exclusion of all other parties. Bangladesh Krishak Sramik Awami League was formed in pursuance of this Constitutional provision. The District Administration Act, 1975 was enacted on the 10th July, 1975 for the administration of districts along totalitarian lines. All newspapers and periodicals except a designated few lost their declaration by the newspapers (Amendment of Declaration) Act. 1975 made on the 19th July, 1975. Multiple political parties and independent newspapers and periodicals lost their existence before Martial Law was proclaimed on the 15th August, 1975 (page-55-56). 

 "It is thus a great irony of history that while the elected representatives of the people in a democratic dispensation banned all political parties, it was a Judge (Mr Justice ASM Sayem) and later a General (Major-General Ziaur Rahman, Bir-Uttam who, under the cover of Martial Law, restored the multi- party system." Page-56. "By the Second Proclamation Order No.1 of 1977 (27th November. 1977). Major-General Ziaur Rahman restored with some changes the original Articles 94 -113 of the Constitution with effect from 1-12-77 and the Supreme Court again started functioning with two Divisions, as originally provided with one common Chief Justice." 

 94. Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, in his book referred to abov, while dealing with "Independence of the exercise of Judicial functions" at page 32 quoted the Article 94(4) of the Constitution which provides, "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution the Chief Justice and the other Judges shall be independent in the exercise of their Judicial functions" and observed that "there is no analogous corresponding provision in the Indian Constitution or. the Constitution of Pakistan" (1973). 

 126. In the case of M Salimullah vs Justice Mohammad Abdur Rouf, reported in 1 BLC 227 their Lordships found that "neither the office of the Judge and nor that of Chief Election Commissioner is an office of profit or emolument as contemplated under clause (3) of Article 147 and that the office of the persons enumerated in Article 147(3) have been clearly distinguished from the office of persons enumerated in Article 147(4) and, for that matter, from the office of persons in the service of the Republic." 

 160. Had the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain written the impugned letter to the District Magistrate. Dhaka informing him about appointment of Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in-Charge of the Daily Ittefaq some time before 23-6-1996 i-e the date on which he entered upon the office of a Minister for the second time, the same would remain beyond the purview of Article 147(3). But he appointed Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in-Charge M the Daily lttefaq and wrote the letter of information thereof to the District Magistrate, Dhaka after assuming the office of a Minister when disqualifying Article 147(3) came into play on him. Under section 2(d) of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 "editor" means the person who controls the selection of the matter that is published in a newspaper. 'Controlling' and 'Selecting' matter to be published in a newspaper is a managerial function relating to the management of the newspaper. The fact of appointing an Editor-in-charge in a newspaper and writing letter in that regard to the District Magistrate was, in fact, taking part in the management or conduct of the Company, association or body having' profit or gain as its object within the meaning of Article 147(3). The innuendo of the term 'in charge' was that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain was the actual editor which he was debarred under the mandatory provision of Article 147(3) and, as such, illegal, void without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 162. In response to the submissions of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the petitioner has placed reliance upon the case of Shahid Nabi Malik vs Chief Election Commissioner, reported in PLD 1997(SC) 32 where their Lordships held that "if an office is a regular office on the strength of the department concerned to which salary/emoluments/ allowances are attached, it is an office of profit. A person cannot change the character/nature of such an office by not drawing salary, etc." 

 179. Scope and field of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is far more wider than any known Constitution. The reason is obvious. The intention of the framers of the Constitution is articulate and vivid both in expression and meaning. A Judge of the Supreme Court, for instance, if holds a post of a director of a private Limited Company engaged in business for making profit or indulges himself in business affairs while holding the office of a Judge the result is disastrous. So also the case of the President, Prime Minister, Chief Adviser, Speaker or Deputy Speaker, Minister, Adviser, Minister for State. Deputy Minister, etc. whose offices have been specified in Clause (4) of Article 147. The Constitutional offices, in that case, will soon become business offices of profit at the peril of the nation. The specified office holders in the intention of the framers of the Constitution shall devote to the fullest extent and the utmost of their ability to the performance of functions in connection with offices to which they have taken Oath free from all other interests or considerations. 

 Mr Justice Abdul Kadir Sheikh had been a Judge of the Pakistan Supreme Court. By Gazette Notification dated 22-1-1975 he was appointed as the Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan on deputation. Amongst others, the Gazette Notification provided during the period Mr Justice Abdul Kadir Sheikh holds the office of Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan he will continue to retain his lien on the office of and seniority as Judge of the Supreme Court. "In a Writ of quo warranto this matter came up for examination and their Lordships held that "Holding of one permanent post precludes the incumbent from holding another post in similar capacity. Respondent Judge admitted by Federal Government to have been appointed as permanent Chief Justice and not as acting Chief Justice. Words on deputation in the Notification and the Paragraph of notification stating that such Judge will continue to retain his lien on the office and seniority as Judge of the Supreme Court is mere surplusage". 

 Their Lordships further held that "None can hold two substantive offices at same time. Supreme Court Judge appointed as Chief Justice of the High Court deemed to have vacated office of the Judge of the Supreme Court". 

 Since we have differed with each other, let the record of the case be placed before the learned Chief Justice for necessary order. 

 MA Aziz J: Rules in the above three Writ petitions were heard and disposed of by judgment and order dated 29-1-2003 by a Division Bench comprised of Mr Joynul Abedin and Mr Abdus Salam Mamun JJ and since those ended in a dissenting judgment, the matters have been sent to me by the Hon'ble Chief Justice for a decision. 

 200. In Writ Petition No.3834 of 1999 Rule was issued on 5-10-1999 at the instance of Mr Mainul Hosein, Executive Director-l as petitioner No. 1 and the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited as petitioner No.2. In this writ petition the sole respondent is Mr Anwar Hossain who wrote a letter on 23-1-1999 (Annexure-A) describing himself as the publisher and addressed the same to Mr Md Habibullah, Senior Security Officer of the daily Ittefaq, telling him that he has not been properly performing his duty as security officer and that he got himself engaged in some other works which are against the discipline of the institution and accordingly, debarred him from coming to office from 24-1-1999. By Annexure-A (I) an order dated 18-8-1999 under the heading "OFFICE ORDER", Mr Anwar Hossain passed the following order "Henceforth Mr Shaukat Hossain Masum, Senior Reporter, shall be in charge of the Finance page of the daily Ittefaq until further orders." and by Annexure-A(2) dated 25-9-1999 under the heading “অফিস নির্দেশ” once again Mr Anwar Hossain describing himself as the publisher with copy to all Directors, the Chief Manager, the Commercial Manager. Acting Editor, News Editor, Mr Monowarul Islam, Chief Accountant, all heads of departments and the leaders of the three workers unions, informed all concerned that on the 8th of December, 1994 the Executive Director-I (Mr Mainul Hosein) without the consent of the Board of Directors dismissed the Chief Accountant Mr Monowarul Islam which was objected to by him (Mr Anwar Hossain) contending that the order of dismissal was without jurisdiction of the Executive Director-I, inasmuch as the said act of dismissal was beyond the power of the Executive Director-I since it is against the provisions of Article 80(B) of the Articles of Association of the Company, that Mr Mainjil Hosein, as plaintiff, instituted a suit in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge 3rd Court. Dhaka in 1995 and obtained an order of injunction. that on 18-7-1999 the said suit was dismissed for default and, in that view of the matter, Mr Monowarul Islam is hereby reinstated as the Chief Accountant of the Daily Ittefaq. 

 (a) to acquire and take over as a company concerned any other undertaking engaged in business, etc. Article 5 provided that to carry on all kinds of business as printer, publishers, stationers order suppliers, etc. Article 6 provided that to carry on all or any of the business of block makers, photographers, etc. Article 7 provided that to carry on the business of manufacturers and distributors, etc. etc. Article 8 provided that to carry on the business of advertising agents, etc. etc. and Article 9 provided that to carry on the business of paper makers and printing, etc. etc. In addition to those articles, some other Articles i.e. 17, 21 and 23, were also referred to. Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque contended that there cannot be any dispute, debate or doubt that Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited is a company incorporated under the Companies Act and is undoubtedly, engaged in making profit and gain, that Mr Anwar Hossain is the Executive Director-II while Mr Mainul Hosein is the Executive Director, that both of them are holding posts or' profit in the Daily Ittefaq, that the post of executive directors which are designed to be a mini board are, without a shred of doubt, posts of profits inasmuch as by the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 the post and position of the Editor. Deputy Editor, Joint Editor, Assistant Editor. Executive Editor News Editor Assistant Editor. Managing Editor, feature editor, special correspondent and that of City Editor were included in Special "Grade-I and so were the posts of managing editor and chief editor, chief correspondent, senior correspondent, senior special correspondent and news editor and the salary for the special grade of officers were fixed at Taka 7,000-2,501-1,00,001 and under the heading নতুন বেতনক্রম Taka 1,100-400-1,700 while under the heading বৃদ্ধির হার 57.14% and by subsequent resolution of the Ittefaq Group of Publications, house rent and other benefits were also enhanced and hence it would be a futile exercise to say that the purpose of the concerned paper is not to make profit or gain or that Mr Anwar Hossain and Mr Mainul Hosein are not holding any post of profit in the Daily Ittefaq. 

 213. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq submits that the post and position of the Editor and Executive Director are not posts of profit. In reply to this contention, Mr Imam has taken us through the resolution book of the company and referred to minutes of an Extraordinary meeting of the Board at Directors held in May 1979. It was unanimously decided that the Executive Director would receive a monthly remuneration of Taka 12,500 and the other Directors shall receive Taka 5000 each month and the remuneration of the Chairman shall be Taka 5000 per month. He has also taken us through the First Wage Board Award, 1997 dated 29th of May. 1997 showing that an Editor of the newspaper has been placed in special grade-1 together with Deputy/ Joint/Assistant and Executive Editors and their salary has been fixed at Taka 7,000 - 250 - 10,000 under the heading "Bartaman Betan Crom" (বর্তমান বেতনক্রম) showing an increase of 57.14% under the heading (বৃদ্ধির হার)  To counter this argument, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that, Mr Anwar Hossain does not draw his salary. In reply to this Mr Akhtar Imam argued that the restrictions and prohibitions envisaged under Article 147(3) of the Constitution comes into operation the moment a person who had been holding any post of profit becomes a Minister, etc. irrespective of whether or not he draws any salary. The parameter is not whether salary is drawn or not. Rather it is as to whether the post or position carries or does not carry salary. From the resolution and from the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 referred to above it is found that the post of Editor and that of the Executive Director are posts of profit. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq then' argued that the proviso to Article 147(3) of the Constitution has rather removed the disqualification of Minister to hold any post of profit as it applies only to future post or position of profit and not the post and position he has been holding prior to his becoming a minister. Thus, according to him, a Minister can retain his former post and position, but cannot hold any post or position of profit once he becomes a Minister. Mr Akhtar Imam, on the other hand, argues that if this contention be accepted then there will be two categories of Ministers, which he submits is an absurd proposition. Mr Huq then argued that the bar or disqualification imposed under Article 147(3) is only directory in nature and that it is not mandatory because no consequence has been provided for or spelt out in the Article. Mr Akhtar Imam argued that prohibitive or negative word in a statute or Article cannot be directory in nature. It must be mandatory and in support of his contention has placed reliance on the case of Osman Gani Mondol vs Mainuddin Ahmed and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 61 and the case of Akbar Hossain vs Government of Pakistan and another reported in PLD 1976 (SC) 315. In the case of Osman Gani Mondal their Lordships held with reference to Crawford's Statutory Constructions page 516, section 261 that it is the Rule of Statutory Construction that where a Statute is framed in terms of command, and there is no indication from the nature of wording of the Act or the surrounding circumstances itself to receive a permissive interpretation, it would be construed as peremptory and again, in section 263 at page 520 thereof it has been said- "prohibitive or negative words can rarely, if ever, be directory, or, as it has been aptly stated, there is but one way to obey the command "thou shall not" and that is to completely refrain from doing the forbidden act and this is so, even though the statute provides no penalty for its disobedience. Accordingly, negative; prohibitory and exclusive words or terms are indicative of the legislative intent that statute is to be mandatory. In the case of Akbar Hossain where a Justice of the Supreme Court was appointed as the Chief Justice of a Province it was held that none could hold two substantive offices at the same time. When a Supreme Court Judge was appointed as Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan it was held that it must be kept in mind that the rule of interpretation of Constitution and mainly the provisions in it entailing disabilities, should be strictly construed. There is no question of the respondent (meaning the Chief Justice of Sind and Baluchistan) holding the two permanent offices of a Judge of Supreme Court and the Chief Justice of High Court, for such a situation is neither contemplated under the Constitution nor is it factually true as it is evident from the reply of the Ministry of Law, Government of Pakistan. Even as regards others the holding of two offices simultaneously will lead to confusion for the terms and conditions of the two are different as regards age of retirement, remuneration pension, etc. The High Court Judge on appointment as Judge of the Supreme Court ceased to be a Judge of the High Court and the High Court Judge in such case does not resign from the office of Judge of the High Court. But his conduct in accepting office of Judge of the Supreme Court amounts to resignation from the former office and appointment of Supreme Court Judge as Chief Justice of a High Court amounts to resignation from office of Judge of Supreme Court and hence, the appointment does not fall within the mischief of Article 107(1)(a) and that if the Chief Justice of a High Court is ever to revert to Supreme Court such would be a fresh appointment and not in continuation of previous appointment. If the interpretation of Mr Huq that the prohibition applies to future posts of profit and not previous posts and that the prohibition is not mandatory and is only directory be accepted then Article 147(3) would be meaningless. Article 147(3) cannot be a dead letter because no provision of the Constitution is irrelevant or redundant. Mr Abdur Razzaque argued that each and every Article of the Constitution shall have the same force and binding character and effect because it is the Supreme Law of the land as it reflects the will of the people (Article 7). 

 215. Mr Huq has also cited the case of M Salimullah, Advocate vs Md Abdur Rouf, Chief Election Commissioner and others reported in 1 BLC 229. In the reported case Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause under what authority Mr Rouf was holding the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and also to show cause under what authority he was at the same time holding the office of Chief Election Commissioner of Bangladesh. In the said case, it was held that Mr Justice Abdur Rouf ceased to be the Chief Election Commissioner on 18-4-1995 and returned to his previous post as a Judge of the High Court Division on 19-6-1995 and later on was elevated to the Appellate Division on 19-6-1995 and is now functioning as a Judge of the Appellate Division and, as such, the cause of action regarding the holding of two posts simultaneously for which the Rule was issued does not subsist now as Mr Justice Rouf is not occupying office which was called in question in the Rule on the date when the Writ of quo warranto was issued. It was also held that the post of a Judge of the Supreme Court is not a post of profit. So, this case has no applicability in the present context. 

 225. For the sake of convenience, before going into the other arguments of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, I propose to discuss the 4 (four) following arguments advanced by him even at the risk of some repetition. The first argument is, that the Rules in Writ Petition Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are not maintainable under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution. Because the impugned acts by Mr Anwar Hossain were not done in the exercise of his powers and functions in the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority rather, if at all, those were done in relation to the affairs of the daily Ittefaq which is a private limited company. In support of this argument, Mr Huq referred to the case of Sultana Nahar, Advocate vs Bangladesh and others reported in 1998 BLD 363. It was a case involving the eviction of 600 sex workers from a brothel called "Kandu Patti" by an unruly mob led by the local ward commissioner, one Mr Hossain, under the very nose of the law enforcing agencies and the Senior Judge made the Rule absolute declaring that the sex workers were illegally and forcibly evicted and the law enforcing agencies failed to discharge their legal duties by not giving legal protection to them (sex workers) to continue their profession at "Kandu Patti" with a direction to respondent Nos. 1, 2, 8 and 9 to earmark a specified and distinct area for their permanent rehabilitation. There was also a mandatory injunction as a stopgap arrangement to restore possession of the evicted sex workers till their rehabilitation, with a further direction to respondent No.5, officer-in-charge, Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka to lodge an FIR, according to the written complaint of 14 sex workers. This was dissented to by the learned Junior Judge holding, inter alia, that the manner of eviction of the sex workers though is condemnable, this Court, in its writ jurisdiction, is unable to restore their possession because, the place is owned by a private individual and that the Government has now lost its jurisdiction to rehabilitate the sex workers since the action done was not in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority attracting the mischief of Article 102(1 )(9). This decision, I am afraid, cannot be made applicable in the instant case simply because the eviction was carried out by some unruly mob led by the local Ward Commissioner who was neither a person exercising any function in the Affairs of the Republic nor did do anything in discharge of his public duty. 

 from 28-12-1993 to 13-1-1994 he (Mr Anwar Hossain) had violated Article 39 of the Constitution and that brought his action fairly and squarely within the ambit of both Article 102(1) and 102(2) and the writ petition cannot be said to be not maintainable. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that Mr Anwar Hossain did, if at all, do something in connection with the affairs of the Ittefaq and not in connection with the Affairs of the Republic or any local body or authority. True it is that the actions of Mr Anwar Hossain primarily affected the affairs of the company, but at the same time it did affect the readers of the paper who have a right to read fair, neutral objective and impartial news and views which is guaranteed under Article 39(2)(b) of the Constitution. It is inescapable to avoid the mischief of Article 39 which is one of the Articles under Chapter III i.e. fundamental rights and hence, there is an infringement of fundamental right under Article 102 which can be invoked by operation or Article 44 of the Constitution. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq also argued that the post of Executive Editor is not a post of profit and, as such, there can be no bar in holding this post while Mr Anwar Hossain became a Minister. I have already dealt with this point that from a plain reading of the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 it is evident that the said post is a post of profit. Mr Akhtar Imam has taken me through the Articles and Memorandum of Association of the company and with reference to Article 50 argued that the directors may from time to time appoint anyone of their body as the Managing Director provided that the Director shall not take any appointment made or committee constituted under Articles 51 and 52. Article 51 deals with managing agent stating that the directors may at any time appoint agent to manage the entire affairs of the company under the control and direction of the directors upon such terms as they think fit subject to the provisions of this Act provided the director shall not make any appointment under this Article during the subsistence of any appointment made or committee constituted under Article 50 and/or 52. Article 52 deals with Executive Committee and Executive Directors, Providing that company in general meeting may appoint from amongst directors one or more directors to be Executive Director or Directors and may constitute an Executive Committee consisting of such executive director/directors as it thinks fit. Provided that no appointment of an Executive Director shall be made or constitution of an Executive Committee shall be made during the subsistence of any appointment earlier made under Article 50 and/or 51. While clause (d) provides that for the purpose of division of responsibility between Executive Directors, the company's business shall be taken to comprise of the following sections: 

 Finally, I wish to express my full agreement with the main judgment prepared by the learned Chief Justice."
